questions.question: Which of the following best describes the physical structure of a basic pinhole camera?
options: An empty, closed box with a tiny hole on the front face and a screen on the back face.
A solid glass cylinder with a convex lens at one end and an eyepiece at the other.
A box containing two parallel plane mirrors set at 45-degree angles.
A closed box with a large aperture on the front and a magnifying glass on the back.

questions.question: How does light travel from a source to the screen at the back of a pinhole camera?
options: In curved paths that bend around the edges of the pinhole
In straight lines from the light source, through the pinhole, to the screen
By reflecting off the inner sides of the camera box multiple times
In waves that expand outward and fill the entire camera volume evenly

questions.question: What is the effect of poking several extra holes into the front face of a pinhole camera?
options: The single image becomes much sharper and brighter.
The image on the screen becomes upright instead of inverted.
Multiple separate images are produced on the screen.
No light can reach the screen, resulting in total darkness.

questions.question: If you widen the tiny hole of a pinhole camera, what will happen to the image formed on the screen?
options: It will become dimmer and sharper.
It will become brighter but more blurred.
It will become inverted and much smaller.
It will remain exactly the same because the box size has not changed.

questions.question: If you cover the top half of a camera lens with a piece of black paper, what happens to the image of the object?
options: Only the bottom half of the object's image is formed.
Only the top half of the object's image is formed.
The complete image is still formed, but it becomes dimmer.
The image is completely blocked and cannot be seen.

questions.question: What does a convex lens do to light rays passing through it, and what is the meeting point called?
options: It refracts light rays so they travel more towards each other, meeting at a focus.
It reflects light rays back towards the source, meeting at a virtual center.
It spreads light rays further apart, creating a dispersed field.
It absorbs all the light rays, converting them into heat at the center of the lens.

questions.question: An object is placed 1.5 meters in front of a flat plane mirror. Which of the following describes its reflection?
options: It is twice the size of the object, inverted, and 3 meters behind the mirror.
It is the same size as the object, upright, and 1.5 meters behind the mirror.
It is smaller than the object, upright, and 0.75 meters behind the mirror.
It is the same size as the object, inverted, and 1.5 meters in front of the mirror.

questions.question: When you stand facing a plane mirror and raise your right hand, your reflection appears to raise its left hand. What is this phenomenon called?
options: Vertical refraction
Lateral inversion
Focal divergence
Chromatic dispersion

questions.question: Why is a reflection in a plane mirror classified as a "virtual image"?
options: Because the light rays physically focus and meet at the surface of the mirror.
Because it can be projected directly onto a screen placed behind the mirror.
Because it appears where light rays seem to have come from, not where they actually come from.
Because the image only exists when the object is moving.

questions.question: What determines the specific colour an object appears when it is illuminated by white or coloured light?
options: The speed of the light rays that are absorbed by the object.
The amount of red, green, and blue light that the object reflects.
The distance of the object from the person observing it.
The heat generated by the light waves as they hit the object's surface.

questions.question: If a white piece of paper is illuminated by a pure green spotlight in a dark room, what colour does the paper appear to be?
options: White
Black
Green
Red

questions.question: Why does a black object appear black when illuminated by white light?
options: It reflects only blue and green light while absorbing red light.
It absorbs all colours of light and reflects none.
It refracts all incoming light rays, bending them around its edges.
It splits the white light into a spectrum and transmits it.

questions.question: What path does a ray of light take when it enters a transparent glass block from the air at an angle to the normal?
options: It continues in a perfectly straight line without changing direction.
It reflects directly off the boundary and returns back into the air.
It bends (turns) towards the normal inside the glass.
It bends (turns) away from the normal inside the glass.

questions.question: A ray of light passes through a rectangular glass block with parallel sides. What is the path of the exiting ray compared to the entering ray?
options: It travels in a direction perpendicular to the original ray.
It ends up in its original direction, but displaced to the side.
It is completely reversed back towards the source.
It spreads out into a wide, circular beam of white light.

questions.question: Which three primary colours of light can be mixed together in different proportions to create all other colours of light?
options: Red, yellow, and blue
Cyan, magenta, and yellow
Red, green, and blue
Orange, green, and violet

questions.question: What is produced when equal amounts of all three primary colours of light (red, green, and blue) are mixed together?
options: Black light
White light
Yellow light
Magenta light
